newsitem.title: GERMANY: German jobless rise sparks doubts on economy.
newsitem.headline: German jobless rise sparks doubts on economy.

text.p: An unexpectedly strong rise in seasonally-adjusted unemployment figures for September has cast doubt on the strength of Germany's recent economic recovery, economists and Labour Office officials said on Tuesday.

The increase in unemployment last month took economists by surprise, particularly in the light of a recent round of strong economic indicators that seemed to show the economy continuing to expand after returning to growth in the second quarter.

German manufacturers had seemed more optimistic in recent surveys as German exports continued rising and industry orders remained firm. Exports have gained from exchange rate shifts, which have seen the mark weaken against major currencies.

"The rise in pan-German unemployment of 39,000 completely contradicted expectations of a broadly unchanged jobless level as well as the other monthly German economic indicators," said James Capel economist Robert Prior-Wandesforde in a statement.
He said one explanation could be that "the economy slowed down again in the third quarter" or that "firms do not expect the economic strength of recent months to be sustained".
The Labour Office said the number of people out of work in Germany in September rose to 3.991 million on a seasonally adjusted basis, pushing the jobless rate up to 10.4 percent.

In west Germany adjusted unemployment rose by 34,000 to 2.75 million, The unemployment rate rose to 9.3 percent from 9.1 percent. In east Germany, jobless numbers rose 4,000 to 1.140 million, or an unemployment rate of 15.3 percent.
Germany has been going through a phase of jobless growth and opinions differ sharply over the causes.

"What is necessary is promoting economic growth, a clear reduction in unit wage costs and further elimination of barriers to hiring," said Friedhelm Ost, a Christian Democratic parliamentary deputy and head of the economic committee.

But economists at the DIW institute in Berlin, which do not adhere to the Bundesbank's monetarist approach, say strict monetary policy and the government's austerity measures are choking off the economy and preventing the creation of jobs.
"The key remains monetary policy. It has much less to do with rigidity on the labour market," said Wolfgang Scheremet, DIW's labour market expert.
But economists did not think the labour market data would be enough on its own to cause the Bundesbank to consider lowering official interest rates.

After dipping into recesssion at the end of 1995, the German economy expanded 1.2 percent in second quarter of 1996 from the same 1995 quarter. The government expects growth of up to one percent for the full year.
Economists do not differ much in their forecasts for the year. But, startled by the rise in unemployment, they are reassessing presumptions about the strength of recovery.

"It's certainly a setback for hopes that the recovery is gaining momentum and that economic figures might be revised further upwards," said Rainer Veit, senior economist with Deutsche Bank AG in Frankfurt.
The economy remains too weak to have any significant impact on the job market, Klaus Leven, vice-president of the Labour Office in Nuremburg told Reuters Fiancial Television.
"Only with growth rates of higher than 2.5 percent can you really expect a fundamental change," he said.
While the economy is still far away from growth rates of that magnitude, key economic indicators published recently have supported the view that it expansion is accelerating.
The respected Munich-based Ifo economic research institute last month said business confidence was returning with strong foreign demand that could boost exports.

Trade figures released on Tuesday seemed to support this view. The trade surplus widened to 10.9 billion marks ($7.15 billion) in July from 7.0 billion in June. Exports rose 16.5 percent from the previous month and 4.2 percent from a year ago.

Because jobless data lags other indicators, trailing rather than leading the broader economy, a more optimistic interpretation of the figures could mean that the labour market has not yet caught up with the rest of the economy.
